title: India's Middle East Oil Imports Plunge 27% as Hormuz Crisis Forces Shift to Russia
excerpt: Russian crude now accounts for 41% of India's oil imports after Strait of Hormuz disruptions cut Middle East supplies, with refiners also turning to Brazil, Venezuela and Angola.
body:
• India's oil imports from the Middle East fell 27% to 1.55 million barrels per day in April-June, while Russian supplies rose 8.3% to 2.26 million bpd.
  • Russian crude hit a record 2.64 million bpd in June alone — half of India's total imports — as the Strait of Hormuz remained largely shut.
  • India's crude import bill surged 61% to $49.8 billion despite a 4% drop in volumes, driven by prices above $100 a barrel for most of the quarter.
  • Indian Oil Corp. and Mangalore Refinery have suspended crude loadings from Iraq as attacks on tankers make Hormuz transit too dangerous.

India's oil supply map underwent a dramatic redraw in the April-to-June quarter as the Strait of Hormuz crisis forced the world's third-largest crude importer to lean harder on Russia, Latin America and West Africa, according to industry data reported by Reuters.

Middle East oil imports fell roughly 27% to 1.55 million barrels per day during the quarter — the first of India's 2026-27 fiscal year — while shipments from the Commonwealth of Independent States, led by Russia, climbed 8.3% to 2.26 million bpd. The shift accelerated sharply in June, when Russian imports surged to a record 2.64 million bpd, up 37.4% from May and accounting for half of India's total intake of 5.24 million bpd.

Hormuz Shutdown Rewrites the Supply Map

The Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman that carried roughly a fifth of global oil supplies before the conflict, has been effectively paralysed since the U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran triggered hostilities in late February. Russia's share of India's imports rose to 41% from 38% a year earlier; the Middle East's share dropped to 31% from 41.4%.

Indian refiners also raised imports from Brazil, Venezuela and Angola to secure heavier crude grades during the quarter. Saudi Arabia managed to supply 403,000 bpd in June, routing shipments through the Red Sea port of Yanbu, which bypasses Hormuz entirely.

A $49.8 Billion Bill Despite Lower Volumes

The supply disruption hit India's pocketbook hard. The country's crude import bill surged 61% to $49.8 billion in the quarter even as total volumes fell 4% to 59.8 million tonnes, according to data from the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell. Brent crude stayed above $100 a barrel for much of the period, peaking at $126.41 on April 30 before easing to the low $80s by late June as a brief ceasefire temporarily calmed markets.

"The country's crude import bill surged 61% to $49.8 billion in the quarter even as total volumes fell 4% to 59.8 million tonnes, according to data from the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell."

India's average crude import price came in at $114.48 a barrel in April, $106.23 in May and $83.22 in June, reflecting the gradual de-escalation before tensions flared again in July, according to Outlook Business.

Refiners Walk Away From Iraqi Crude

The danger in the Strait has grown acute enough to halt specific shipments. Indian Oil Corp., the country's largest refiner, abandoned plans to load the VLCC Lila Jamnagar from Iraq, concluding that sending a 2-million-barrel tanker through Hormuz was no longer worth the risk, Bloomberg reported. Mangalore Refinery & Petrochemicals has also suspended Iraqi liftings.

Iraq had been one of India's largest suppliers under long-term contracts that require the buyer to arrange shipping — an obligation that becomes untenable when tankers face missile strikes. India's shipping ministry has instructed shipowners not to deploy Indian seafarers on vessels transiting Hormuz until further notice.

What Comes Next

The outlook has darkened since a fragile U.S.-Iran ceasefire collapsed in early July, reviving heavy exchanges of strikes and choking off Hormuz traffic once more. Yemen's Houthi militia have opened a new front by threatening to blockade Saudi shipping in the Bab el-Mandeb strait, potentially cutting off the Yanbu workaround.

"Indian refineries' dependence on oil imports from Russia, West Africa and the Americas is expected to rise if supplies from the Strait continue to be paralysed and Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis impose a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia."

— Sources at Indian refiners, via Reuters

Refiner sources told Reuters that one fallback would be to import Saudi oil via the Cape of Good Hope, adding weeks to voyage times and significant cost. For now, Moscow remains the path of least resistance: Indian refiners continue to buy from non-sanctioned Russian entities even after Washington withdrew a temporary sanctions waiver.

For India's 1.4 billion consumers, the calculus is simple but uncomfortable. The country imports more than 85% of its crude, and every sustained $10 increase in Brent adds roughly $15 billion to the annual import bill. With Brent back above $90 this week on renewed U.S. strikes against Iran, the pressure on India's current account deficit and inflation — already at 4.38% in June — is unlikely to ease soon.

nri_angle: India's surging oil import bill and supply chain disruption threaten higher fuel prices and inflation that directly affect household budgets and remittance purchasing power for the diaspora.
